title: Land & documents
headline: Make sure the land is yours — on paper — before any money goes into the ground.
seoTitle: Buying land in Nigeria from abroad: C of O, survey plan and building approval
seoDescription: Plain-English guide for Nigerians abroad: how to check title (C of O, R of O), survey plans and building approval in Abuja and Lagos before you build.
summary: Title, survey and approval are the foundation under the foundation. Most diaspora losses happen here, not on site.
duration: 4–12 weeks for searches and survey; building approval commonly 1–3 months in Abuja (AMMC/DRD) or Lagos (LASPPPA/LASBCA) [CHECK current timelines]
whatHappens: Title search: a lawyer checks the land registry (AGIS in Abuja; Lagos Land Registry) that the seller actually owns the plot and it is free of disputes, government acquisition or other claims.

Documents you should end up with: Certificate of Occupancy (C of O) or Right of Occupancy (R of O) / allocation letter; Deed of Assignment; Governor’s Consent (Lagos) or Minister’s Consent (FCT) where land changes hands; registered survey plan. [CHECK which apply to your plot]
Survey: a registered surveyor (SURCON) produces or verifies the survey plan and plants beacons at the corners. The beacon numbers on site must match the survey plan.
Site visit and charting: confirm the plot on the ground is the plot on the paper, and that it is not on a road reserve, drainage channel, setback or government acquisition.

Building plan approval: architectural, structural and services drawings are submitted to the development control authority for approval before work starts. Lagos also requires stage inspections and certificates. [CHECK current Lagos LASBCA stage-certification rules]
Soil test (recommended): a geotechnical investigation tells the structural engineer what foundation the ground needs, especially in waterlogged or filled land.
problems: Same plot sold to several buyers (‘double allocation’). Only an independent lawyer’s registry search protects you.
Survey plan that belongs to a different plot, or beacons moved. Ask for beacon numbers and check them against the plan with your own surveyor.
Land under government acquisition or on a planned road — cheap for a reason, and can be demolished later.
‘Omo onile’ / community levies in Lagos and parts of the South West: extra demands to start work. Get any community agreement in writing. [CHECK local practice for your area]
Starting construction without approval because ‘everybody does it’. Unapproved buildings can be sealed or demolished, and it hurts resale and mortgage value.
Relatives or agents holding the original documents in their own name. Documents should be in your name and the originals kept by you or your lawyer.
questions: Who did the title search, and can I have the written search report from the registry?
Is the C of O / R of O in my name? If not, when will consent and registration be completed?
Who is the surveyor, are they SURCON-registered, and what are the beacon numbers?
Has the building plan been submitted? Can I see the approval letter and approved stamped drawings?
Is a soil test needed for this plot? If not, why not?
Are there any community or ‘development’ levies, and who will pay them?
photoCheckpoints: Clear photos/scans of the C of O or R of O, Deed of Assignment and consent — all pages.
Photos of each corner beacon with its number readable, plus a wide shot showing the plot.
Short video walking the boundary, with a phone GPS/map pin shown on screen.
Photo of the building approval letter and the approval stamp on the drawings.
Registry search report on the lawyer’s letterhead.
